title: A convert in New York (1938)
hook: he reads philosophy, walks into a church, and is baptized

segments.voice: Yesterday, a restless young man: Merton, orphaned, drifting through Cambridge and Columbia. Your line was restless is a start. Where did your restlessness show up? Today it starts to go somewhere. Day two hundred seventy-three.

New York, 1937. Merton is at Columbia, and he buys a book for a class: a history of medieval philosophy. On the train home he opens it and sees the little Latin stamp inside that says a Catholic censor approved it. He's so annoyed he nearly throws it out the window. He doesn't. He reads it. And one idea in it cracks something open. A year later he's standing in a priest's doorway on a rainy afternoon, saying: I want to become a Catholic. Today: how that happened.
screen: `A BOOK HE NEARLY THREW OUT.` → `ONE IDEA CRACKS IT OPEN.` → `I WANT TO BECOME A CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. The book was Étienne Gilson's The Spirit of Medieval Philosophy. Merton had assumed God was a vague, fuzzy feeling. Gilson showed him the medieval idea that God is not one more thing in the universe, but being itself, the reason anything exists at all. Merton later wrote that this gave him a whole new respect for the faith. Second, the friends. A professor named Mark Van Doren, a poet friend named Robert Lax. And a surprise: a Hindu monk visiting New York, called Bramachari, who told him to read Augustine's Confessions and The Imitation of Christ, the great books of his own Western tradition. Merton never forgot that kindness. Third, the church. One Sunday in August 1938 he went, alone, to Mass at Corpus Christi Church near the university. He left before the end, nervous, and walked down the street feeling happier than he'd felt in years. Then, weeks later, he was reading about the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins becoming a Catholic, and he put the book down, walked through the rain to the rectory, and asked. On November 16, 1938, he was baptized. Fourth, the word. Convert comes from the Latin convertere, to turn around. And here's the Catholic twist: the turning isn't only the person's own work. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him." Looking back, Merton saw it the same way. A book, a teacher, a monk, a Mass. Someone was drawing him the whole time.
screen: `GOD AS BEING ITSELF.` · `A TEACHER, A POET, A HINDU MONK.` · `CORPUS CHRISTI, AUGUST 1938.` · `CONVERTERE — TO TURN AROUND.` · then, large: `EXCEPT THE FATHER DRAW HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember what first drew you. Settle and breathe. Go back to the first time faith, or the question of God, caught your attention. Maybe a person. A place. A song, a funeral, a book you almost threw away. It doesn't matter if you're sure of anything now. Just find that first thread and look at it for a moment. Whose hand was in it? If you pray, you can say thank you for it. The bell holds the time.
Convert. From the Latin convertere, to turn around. For Merton, a turning that took years, through a book, some friends, and one quiet Mass. Today's word.

Your line: someone was drawing him. Look back at this week: where have you hidden, the log in the fire, judged on love, arise and come, the night is a way, then a restless young man turning around. Today, notice one thing that's drawing you. Day two hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Adults who become Catholic today usually walk a path of study and prayer called the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults, and are often baptized or received into the Church at the Easter Vigil.

Baptism date 16 November 1938; confirm. Merton also made his first Communion that day.
